title: Coarsening Linear Non-Gaussian Causal Models with Cycles
claim: Distinct fine-grained structures within a feedback loop are indistinguishable from data, yet they share one identifiable coarse summary graph.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed cluster boxes around cycles, condensed DAG at right
description: Three graph panels are arranged in a row. The left and center panels each show five variable nodes, X1 through X5, drawn as black-outlined circles. Three of the nodes, X2, X3 and X4, form a directed 3-cycle inside a pale pink dashed rounded box labeled π2. The cycle runs X2→X3→X4→X2 in the left panel and the reverse direction in the center panel. In the center panel the nodes are relabeled, so the incoming edge from X1 lands on X4 rather than X2. Thin dashed gray arrows run from X1 into the box and out of the box to X5. The right panel is a vertical chain of three circles, π1→π2→π3, and π2 is tinted pink to match the boxes. The palette is mostly black and white with a faint pink accent, so the eye goes first to the cycles and then to the chain at right.
caption: Distributional equivalence and condensation for the five-variable cyclic SCM of [ref] ([ref]). (left, center) Two members of the distributional equivalence class recovered by ICA, differ only in the orientation of the 3-cycle inside the SCC $\pi_2 = \{X_2, X_3, X_4\}$; both correspond to admissible permutations of the demixing matrix $\widehat W$. (right) The shared condensation $G^{\mathrm{sc}}$ with clusters $\pi_1 = \{X_1\}$, $\pi_2 = \{X_2, X_3, X_4\}$, $\pi_3 = \{X_5\}$. ICA cannot distinguish (left) from (center), but $G^{\mathrm{sc}}$ is identifiable ([ref]). Note that the inter-SCC edge from $X_1$ lands on $X_2$ in (left) and on $X_4$ in (center); the cluster-level edge $\pi_1 \to \pi_2$ of $G^{\mathrm{sc}}$ is unchanged.
abstract: Recent work on causal abstraction, in particular graphical approaches focusing on causal structure between clusters of variables, aims to summarize a high-dimensional causal structure in terms of a low-dimensional one. Existing methods for learning such summaries from data assume that both structures are acyclic. Acyclicity is helpful for causal effect identification and reasoning, but it excludes the many systems of scientific interest that contain feedback loops. We show that in the linear non-Gaussian (LiNG) setting, the acyclicity assumption on the high-dimensional structure can be relaxed while still allowing recovery of a low-dimensional causal directed acyclic graph (DAG). LiNG models with cycles are observationally identifiable only up to an equivalence class whose members differ only within their feedback loops. Our low-dimensional DAG, which is invariant across all members of this class, is therefore identifiable from observational data alone. While existing approaches for learning this equivalence class have exponential time complexity, our low-dimensional summary is learned in worst-case cubic time and comes with finite-sample guarantees. We provide open source code and experiments on synthetic data to corroborate our theoretical results.
